name: Jon Sherman
one_line: A self-taught adult improver turned data-literate golf writer who built Practical Golf into one of the internet's most trusted game-improvement outposts by arguing that amateurs fail at strategy, practice, and expectations far more than at swing mechanics.
bio: Sherman is an American golf writer, coach, and publisher based on Long Island (Port Jefferson, NY), educated at NYU's Stern School of Business, who came to golf as a serious adult improver rather than through the junior-elite or club-pro pipeline — a biography he treats as the whole point of his credibility. He founded the website Practical Golf around 2014–15, writing hundreds of articles from a "player-coach" perspective aimed at the recreational golfer drowning in swing tips, and self-published his first book, 101 Mistakes All Golfers Make (and How to Fix Them), in 2015 through his own imprint, Practical Golf, Inc. His breakthrough came with The Four Foundations of Golf (2022), which became an Amazon #1 golf bestseller and has sold well past 50,000 copies, followed by The Foundations of Winning Golf on competitive play; he also co-hosts the long-running podcast The Sweet Spot with coach Adam Young. He has gone from average player to scratch and then plus-handicap competitor, plays serious amateur tournaments, and now coaches golfers including, by his own description, players at the professional level — his career arc is essentially the case study his books rest on.
known_for: The Four Foundations of Golf (2022) — expectation management, course strategy, practice, and mental game as the four levers of amateur improvement
101 Mistakes All Golfers Make (and How to Fix Them) (2015) — his self-published debut, a plain-language catalogue of recreational golfers' recurring errors
The Foundations of Winning Golf — a guide to competitive and tournament play for amateurs
Practical Golf, the blog/newsletter he founded in the mid-2010s, and its anti-hype editorial stance
The Sweet Spot podcast, co-hosted with Adam Young
Popularizing strokes-gained and shot-dispersion thinking (Broadie, Arccos-style data) for ordinary golfers
"Expectation management" as a performance skill — knowing what a good shot actually is for your handicap
school: The evidence-based / data-informed golf improvement movement — the loose post-Every Shot Counts school that fuses strokes-gained statistics, motor-learning science, and sport psychology against traditional swing-tip instruction. Not an academic tradition; a practitioner-writer tradition.
lineage: He builds openly on Mark Broadie's strokes-gained work (Every Shot Counts), the shot-pattern/strategy thinking associated with Scott Fawcett's DECADE and data analysts like Lou Stagner, Adam Young's motor-learning-driven practice methodology (The Practice Manual), and the acceptance-and-process lineage of golf psychology running from Bob Rotella through contemporaries like Jared Tendler. His own contribution is synthesis and translation rather than original research: he is the popularizer who turned tour-level analytics and coaching science into instructions a 15-handicap can act on Saturday morning. Downstream, he is a template for a generation of newsletter-and-self-publishing golf writers, and his framing ("foundations, not fixes") now circulates widely in golf media and social content, often uncredited.
stance: Golfers waste their improvement on the wrong problem. The swing is the most-discussed and least-tractable variable; the enormous, cheap gains sit in managing expectations (most shots are not going to be good, and knowing that stops the spiral), in course strategy (aiming to the fat side, taking enough club, accepting bogey, avoiding compounding errors), in practicing in ways motor-learning research actually supports (variability, randomness, feedback, intent) rather than beating balls at a static range, and in a mental game built on process and acceptance instead of outcome. Improvement is a long game of compounding habits, not a secret; and the point is to keep enjoying golf for decades, not to chase a fix that lasts three rounds.
blind_spots: He is a self-taught writer-coach without formal PGA teaching credentials, biomechanics training, or research background, and his work is synthesis of other people's science — which means the underlying literature sometimes arrives flattened into confident rules of thumb. His near-total deprioritizing of technique is a genuine limitation: plenty of high handicappers really do have mechanical faults that no amount of strategy or acceptance will offset, and strategy advice extrapolated from tour and aggregate amateur data can transfer poorly to players whose dispersion is wild and inconsistent. "Expectation management" is his best idea and also his most misusable one — it can shade into resignation or a ceiling-setting fatalism, and critics note it is close to unfalsifiable as coaching advice. Everything is self-published, so it has never been through outside editorial or expert vetting, and the whole enterprise (books, newsletter, courses, apparel ambassadorships, affiliate links) is commercially entangled with the recommendations. The 2015 101 Mistakes in particular is early, thin, and listicle-shaped next to his later work — it reads as a blogger's first book, which is what it was.
politics: No discernible political orientation in the public record. Across a decade of blogging, two-plus books, hundreds of podcast episodes, and active social accounts, his output is almost entirely non-political — the closest thing to advocacy is intra-golf: skepticism of equipment marketing, golf media clickbait, distance-obsession, and instruction fads, plus commentary on the professional tours' business disputes. He has not, as far as the public record shows, staked out partisan or ideological positions, and it would be guessing to infer any. Treat him as apolitical in his public work.
public_views: Swing tips are the least efficient path to lower scores; most golfers are one strategy change and one honest expectation away from playing better
Knowing what a realistic shot looks like for your handicap is transformational — it changes emotional reactions and target selection
"Bogey is your friend": avoiding double and triple bogeys matters more for amateurs than making birdies
Aim away from trouble, take more club, stop short-siding yourself — most strokes are lost to compounding bad decisions, not bad swings
Practice should be random, variable, and feedback-rich (face spray, targets, games), not a bucket of 7-irons at a mat
The worst advice golfers pass to each other is well-meaning technical instruction from other amateurs
Enjoyment and longevity are legitimate goals, not consolation prizes — a game that lasts a lifetime beats a two-week breakthrough
Openly skeptical about whether new golf technology and AI coaching tools will actually make amateurs better
Recommends the work of others generously — Adam Young, Jared Tendler, data analysts — and positions himself as translator rather than guru
interview_notes: Measured, unflashy, and conspicuously allergic to guru posturing — he repeatedly disclaims being a swing instructor and frames himself as a fellow player who reads the research. On The Sweet Spot he plays the practical, scoring-focused counterweight to Adam Young's technical and motor-learning depth, and the show's temperament is conversational and hedged rather than declarative, with frequent "it depends on your level." He uses his own tournament rounds as raw material, including candid discussion of nerves, choking, anxiety over specific shots, and slumps — the self-experimentation is the rhetorical engine. Recurring themes: expectations, dispersion, long-term compounding, contempt for clickbait improvement content, and an insistence that the emotional experience of golf is a performance variable, not a soft topic.
personal: Long Island-based (Port Jefferson, NY) with a business-school background (NYU Stern) rather than a golf-industry one — the outsider's analytical framing is baked in. The formative fact is that he was an ordinary golfer who systematically improved to scratch and then plus handicap as an adult, logging what he describes as 10,000-plus hours of practice and study; his books are essentially the reverse-engineering of that project. He built Practical Golf as an independent, self-published operation and still competes in amateur tournaments, which keeps his advice tested under pressure rather than purely theoretical.
